problems.title: A denominator with an absolute value
problems.question: Find the real inputs where $\dfrac{2x-1}{(2x+1)(|9x|-4)(x^2+1)}$ is undefined.
problems.idea: Set each denominator factor equal to zero, keeping only real solutions.
formulas: A fraction is undefined when its denominator is zero.
steps: $x^2+1$ never vanishes for real $x$, so it adds no excluded input.

problems.title: A nested absolute-value equation
problems.question: Find the sum of all solutions of $\big||x|-6\big|=4$.
problems.idea: Remove the outer absolute value first, then the inner one.
steps: The outer equation gives $|x|-6=4$ or $|x|-6=-4$.
Therefore $|x|=10$ or $|x|=2$.
The four solutions are $10,-10,2,-2$. Their sum is $0$.

problems.title: Intercept lengths determine a slope
problems.question: The displayed line crosses the negative $x$-axis at $A$ and the positive $y$-axis at $B$, with $OA=3OB$. Which listed equation can represent it?
problems.idea: Use the signs of the intercepts and their length ratio to find the slope.
formulas: For intercepts $(-u,0)$ and $(0,v)$, the slope is $v/u$.
steps: Write $OB=t>0$, so $OA=3t$. Then $A=(-3t,0)$ and $B=(0,t)$.
The slope is $(t-0)/(0-(-3t))=1/3$. The $y$-intercept must be positive.
Among the choices, $y=\frac13x+2$ has slope $1/3$ and a positive intercept.
Its intercepts are $(-6,0)$ and $(0,2)$, and $6=3\cdot2$.

problems.title: Count weekdays across several months
problems.question: April 1 is a Tuesday. What weekday is November 19 in the same year?
problems.idea: Find the number of elapsed days, then reduce it modulo seven.
formulas: Elapsed days from a month’s first day to the next month’s first day equal that month’s length.
steps: From April 1 to November 1 there are $30+31+30+31+31+30+31=214$ days.
From November 1 to November 19 there are $18$ more, so the total is $232$.
$232=33\cdot7+1$, so the weekday advances by one day.
One day after Tuesday is Wednesday.

problems.title: Last digit of a large expression
problems.question: Find the last digit of $8^{10}-33\cdot52+47^7$.
problems.idea: Compute each term’s last digit and combine them modulo ten.
formulas: Powers of $8$ cycle through $8,4,2,6$; powers of $7$ cycle through $7,9,3,1$.
steps: $10$ leaves remainder $2$ on division by $4$, so $8^{10}$ ends in $4$.
$33\cdot52=1716$ ends in $6$. Here $52$ means fifty-two.
$47^7$ has the same last digit as $7^7$. Since $7$ leaves remainder $3$ modulo $4$, this last digit is $3$.
The expression ends in the residue $4-6+3=1$.
problems.note: The factor in the source is the integer $52$, not $5^2$. Reading it as a square would change the result.

problems.title: Locate an apartment by entrance and floor
problems.question: Each entrance of a fourteen-floor building has four apartments per floor. Find the entrance and floor of apartment 125 in the unanswered paper. The answered paper instead asks about apartment 121.
problems.idea: Count apartments per entrance first, then count within the correct entrance.
steps: The first two entrances contain apartments $1$–$56$ and $57$–$112$. The third starts at $113$.
For apartment $125$, its position in entrance 3 is $125-112=13$. Positions $13$–$16$ are on floor $4$.
For apartment $121$, its position is $121-112=9$. Positions $9$–$12$ are on floor $3$.
problems.answer: Unanswered paper, No. 125: entrance 3, floor 4 (option დ). Answered paper, No. 121: entrance 3, floor 3.
problems.note: The two source versions genuinely use different apartment numbers. This explanation covers both; it does not treat the different floor numbers as an answer-key error.

problems.title: Find a line intersection from a plotted grid
problems.question: Find the sum of the coordinates of the intersection of the two lines in the diagram. The rising line passes through $(-2,-1)$ and $(2,2)$; the falling line passes through $(-1,2)$ and $(2,1)$.
problems.idea: Read exact grid points, form the two line equations, then solve them together.
steps: The rising line has slope $(2-(-1))/(2-(-2))=3/4$. Using $(2,2)$ gives intercept $1/2$, so $y=\frac34x+\frac12$.
The falling line has slope $(1-2)/(2-(-1))=-1/3$. Its intercept is $5/3$, so $y=-\frac13x+\frac53$.
Equate and multiply by $12$: $9x+6=-4x+20$. Thus $13x=14$ and $x=14/13$.
Then $y=\frac34\cdot\frac{14}{13}+\frac12=17/13$.
The required sum is $14/13+17/13=31/13$.

problems.title: A common factor reveals a divisor
problems.question: Which listed number divides $25^9+5^{16}$?
problems.idea: Rewrite both powers with base five and take out the smaller power.
steps: Since $65=13\cdot5$, this equals $65\cdot(2\cdot5^{15})$, so it is divisible by $65$.
Its prime factors are only $2,5,13$, with just one factor $2$. The other choices require a factor $3$, $7$, or at least two factors $2$, so they do not divide it.

problems.title: Prices of skis and skates
problems.question: Three pairs of skis and four pairs of skates cost 47 GEL. Two pairs of skates cost 1 GEL more than one pair of skis. Find the combined price of one pair of each.
problems.idea: Use one variable for each price and translate both purchases into equations.
steps: Let $s$ be the price of one pair of skis and $t$ the price of one pair of skates. Then $3s+4t=47$.
The second condition is $2t=s+1$, or $s=2t-1$.
Substitute: $3(2t-1)+4t=47$, so $10t=50$ and $t=5$.
Then $s=9$, so $s+t=14$ GEL. Check: $3\cdot9+4\cdot5=47$.

problems.title: Fuel remaining after two percentage losses
problems.question: A car uses $25\%$ of its fuel on the first trip, then $20\%$ of the remainder on the second. It has $27$ litres left. How much did it start with?
problems.idea: Successive percentage changes multiply; the second percentage uses the reduced amount.
steps: After the first trip, $75\%$ remains.
After the second, $80\%$ of that remains, so the final fraction is $0.75\cdot0.80=0.60$.
If the initial amount is $F$, then $0.60F=27$. Thus $F=27/0.60=45$ litres.

problems.title: A boat journey with a stop
problems.question: A boat leaves upstream and must return within 5 hours. It travels at $12.5$ km/h in still water; the current is $2.5$ km/h. The group spends 3 hours ashore before returning. What is the greatest possible distance from the dock?
problems.idea: Only two hours are available for travel. The upstream and downstream distances are equal, but the speeds differ.
formulas: $v_{\rm upstream}=v_{rm still}-v_{rm current}$; $v_{\rm downstream}=v_{rm still}+v_{rm current}$.
steps: The upstream speed is $12.5-2.5=10$ km/h; the downstream speed is $12.5+2.5=15$ km/h.
Travel time is $5-3=2$ hours. For one-way distance $d$, use $d/10+d/15=2$.
The left side is $3d/30+2d/30=d/6$, so $d/6=2$ and $d=12$ km.
The journey uses $1.2$ hours upstream and $0.8$ hours downstream, exactly $2$ hours. Any greater distance would exceed the time available.

problems.title: Compare powers of one half
problems.question: Order $a=(1/32)^3$, $b=(1/2)^{10}$, and $c=(1/8)^6$ from smallest to largest.
problems.idea: Rewrite all three with base $1/2$. Larger positive exponents make a number between zero and one smaller.
steps: Since $18>15>10$ and the base is less than $1$, the value order is $c<a<b$.

problems.title: Use the factor theorem
problems.question: For which $p$ is $3x^3-16x^2+9x+p$ divisible by $x+3$?
problems.idea: A polynomial is divisible by $x+3$ exactly when it is zero at $x=-3$.
formulas: Factor theorem: $x-r$ divides $P(x)$ if and only if $P(r)=0$.
steps: Therefore $p=252$.

problems.title: Expand and cancel before evaluating
problems.question: Evaluate $9a^3-a(3a+2)^2+4a(3a+7)+(3a-2)^2$ at $a=1/3$.
problems.idea: Expand the squares and collect like powers. Many terms cancel.
formulas: Terms with the same variable powers can be combined by adding their coefficients.
steps: Adding all terms gives $9a^2+12a+4=(3a+2)^2$.

problems.title: Order of operations with signed fractions
problems.question: Compute $(-3)^2-11-(+2)\div(-1/12)+(-12)\cdot\frac23\cdot2$.
problems.idea: Do powers, division and multiplication before combining the signed terms.
formulas: Dividing by a nonzero fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.
$(\text{negative})\times(\text{positive})$ is negative; subtracting a negative adds its opposite.
steps: $(+2)\div(-1/12)=2(-12)=-24$, so subtracting this term adds $24$.
The total is $9-11+24-16=6$.

problems.title: A named angle between two altitudes
problems.question: In isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB=BC$, the altitude lines $AD$ and $CE$ meet at $M$. Given $\angle AMC=48^\circ$, find $\angle BAC$.
problems.idea: For this isosceles triangle, the angle between altitude rays towards the base vertices is twice a base angle.
steps: The equal sides meet at $B$, so the equal base angles are at $A$ and $C$.
The altitudes are perpendicular to the two equal sides. The angle between their rays towards $A,C$ is the supplement of the apex angle: $\angle AMC=180^\circ-B$.
Combining this with $B=180^\circ-2A$ gives $\angle AMC=2A$.
Thus $48^\circ=2A$, so $A=24^\circ$. The remaining angles are $C=24^\circ$ and $B=132^\circ$.

problems.title: How many intersections can four lines have?
problems.question: Four distinct lines have no parallel pair. What numbers of distinct intersection points are possible?
problems.idea: Count pairwise intersections and consider which can coincide at a common point.
formulas: Three concurrent lines account for three line pairs at one point.
steps: If no three lines are concurrent, all six pairwise intersections are distinct: $6$ points.
If exactly three lines meet at one point, their three pairs give one point; the fourth line meets those three at three further distinct points. Total: $1+3=4$.
If all four are concurrent, there is only $1$ point.
Any coincidence of pair intersections means at least three lines are concurrent. With four lines, that leads to either the three-line or four-line case above, so there are no other totals.

problems.title: Sum the marked exterior angles
problems.question: Find the sum of the six marked angles in the diagram formed by extending the sides of a triangle. At each vertex, the two marked vertical angles are exterior angles.
problems.idea: Each marked pair contributes twice the supplement of that vertex’s interior angle.
formulas: If a triangle angle is $A$, an adjacent exterior angle is $180^\circ-A$.
steps: Call the triangle’s interior angles $A,B,C$.
The two marked angles at the first vertex total $2(180^\circ-A)$; similarly the other pairs total $2(180^\circ-B)$ and $2(180^\circ-C)$.
The overall sum is $2[540^\circ-(A+B+C)]$.
Using the triangle sum, this becomes $2(540^\circ-180^\circ)=720^\circ$.
problems.note: The multiple arcs distinguish angle markings; each marked angle is counted once. There are two marked exterior angles at each of the three vertices, not just one.

problems.title: Use two circles and the same pair of lines
problems.question: Two nonintersecting chords $AB,CD$ of one circle lie on lines tangent to a second circle. The first circle has far arc $BD=70^\circ$. The second circle’s minor arc between tangencies is $154^\circ$. Find the small near arc $AC$ of the first circle.
problems.idea: The angle between the two lines can be computed from either circle.
steps: For the second circle, the angle between the tangent rays is $180^\circ-154^\circ=26^\circ$.
For the first circle, those same rays are secants, so $26^\circ=\frac12(70^\circ-\widehat{AC})$.
Multiply by $2$: $52^\circ=70^\circ-\widehat{AC}$.
Thus $\widehat{AC}=18^\circ$.

problems.title: A parallelogram inside an isosceles triangle
problems.question: In isosceles triangle $ABC$, $AB=BC=12$ cm. Point $D$ is on base $AC$. Lines through $D$ parallel to $BC$ and $AB$ meet $AB,BC$ at $E,F$. Find the perimeter of $DEBF$.
problems.idea: Parallel lines give a parallelogram and a smaller isosceles triangle.
formulas: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
Angles formed by parallel lines are equal.
Equal angles in a triangle have equal opposite sides.
steps: Because $DE\parallel BF$ and $DF\parallel EB$, quadrilateral $DEBF$ is a parallelogram.
In triangle $AED$, angle $EAD$ equals base angle $A$ of $ABC$ and angle $ADE$ equals base angle $C$. These are equal, so $AE=DE$.
Along side $AB$, $AE+EB=12$. Substituting $AE=DE$ gives $DE+EB=12$.
The parallelogram perimeter is $2(DE+EB)=24$ cm.

problems.title: Every angle is smaller than the other two together
problems.question: Every angle of a triangle is smaller than the sum of the other two. What type of triangle must it be?
problems.idea: Replace “the other two angles” with the difference from 180 degrees.
formulas: A triangle is acute if every angle is less than $90^\circ$.
steps: The condition for $A$ says $A<B+C=180^\circ-A$.
Thus $2A<180^\circ$, so $A<90^\circ$.
The same argument gives $B<90^\circ$ and $C<90^\circ$.
All three angles are acute.

problems.title: An interior angle equals a difference of exterior angles
problems.question: One interior angle of a triangle equals the positive difference of the two exterior angles at the other vertices. What type of triangle must it be?
problems.idea: The two exterior angles are supplements of their interior angles.
steps: Name the given interior angle $A$. The difference of the other exterior angles is $|(180^\circ-B)-(180^\circ-C)|=|C-B|$.
Suppose $C\ge B$; the other order is identical after swapping names. Then $A=C-B$, so $A+B=C$.
But $A+B+C=180^\circ$. Substituting $A+B=C$ gives $2C=180^\circ$.
Therefore $C=90^\circ$. In the opposite ordering, $B=90^\circ$. Either way the triangle is right-angled.

problems.title: A triple-angle relationship from equal lengths
problems.question: In the diagram, $AB$ is a diameter of a circle with centre $O$, and $C$ lies beyond $A$. A secant from $C$ meets the circle at near point $E$ and far point $D$. Given $CE=OA$, how many times as large is $\angle BOD$ as $\angle AOE$?
problems.idea: Use two isosceles triangles: $OE=CE$ and $OE=OD$.
formulas: All radii of a circle are equal.
An isosceles triangle has equal base angles.
Triangle angles sum to $180^\circ$; adjacent angles on a line also sum to $180^\circ$.
steps: Write $\theta=\angle AOE$. Since $OC$ points along $OA$, $\angle COE=\theta$.
$OE=OA=CE$, so triangle $OEC$ is isosceles and $\angle OCE=\theta$. Its third angle is $\angle OEC=180^\circ-2\theta$.
Rays $EC$ and $ED$ are opposite, hence $\angle OED=2\theta$. In isosceles triangle $OED$, $OE=OD$, so $\angle EDO=2\theta$ and $\angle EOD=180^\circ-4\theta$.
In the displayed order, $\angle COD=\angle COE+\angle EOD=180^\circ-3\theta$.
Rays $OC$ and $OB$ are opposite. Thus $\angle BOD=180^\circ-\angle COD=3\theta$.
problems.answer: $\angle BOD$ is three times $\angle AOE$ (option ა).

problems.title: A triangle’s possible perimeters
problems.question: Two sides of a triangle are $5$ cm and $9$ cm. Which listed perimeter is impossible: $18.7,25.4,27.9,20,22,28.3$ cm?
problems.idea: Bound the third side using the strict triangle inequality, then add the two known sides.
steps: The third side must satisfy $4<c<14$.
Adding $14$ gives the perimeter range $18<P<28$.
All listed numbers except $28.3$ lie strictly inside that interval.
$28.3$ would require $c=14.3$, exceeding $5+9=14$, so it cannot form a triangle.

problems.title: Subtract two perimeters
problems.question: Point $D$ lies on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$, with $\angle CAD=\angle ACD$. The perimeters of $ABC$ and $ABD$ are $37$ cm and $24$ cm. Find $AC$.
problems.idea: The equal angles make triangle $ACD$ isosceles, so a perimeter difference cancels two lengths.
formulas: Equal angles have equal opposite sides.
Perimeter of a triangle is the sum of its side lengths.
steps: In triangle $ACD$, $\angle CAD=\angle ACD$ implies $CD=AD$.
Subtract the perimeters: $37-24=(AB+BC+AC)-(AB+BD+AD)$.
Cancel $AB$ and use $BC-BD=DC$: the right side becomes $DC+AC-AD$.
Since $DC=AD$, this reduces to $AC$. Thus $AC=13$ cm.
